How long have you been in this market?

People always ask what the hardest part of going international is and they expect me to say the language or the taxes. It is neither. The hardest part is that you arrive with nothing. At home we have built up a track record over twelve years, we have never had to introduce ourselves, business comes through word of mouth. You land in a new country and none of that exists. I have sat in meetings where I could see the person opposite me deciding whether we were real, and I had no way to prove it except by turning up again. We have expanded into three markets now and the pattern has been identical every single time. Year one is embarrassing. Year two is slow. Year three, somebody you helped two years ago mentions your name in a room you are not in, and that is the moment it starts.

I have been in this job for nine years and I have almost never applied for anything. That sounds like luck and partly it is, but the honest version is that I have said yes to a lot of things that were not my job. The first time somebody asked me to fly out and present to a client overseas, I had never done it, I had no idea what I was doing, and I said yes on the phone before I could think about it. That was the turning point, although it did not feel like one at the time. It felt like a bad week. Since then almost every good thing has come through somebody who was in one of those rooms. My career has not been a plan. It has been a very steady accumulation of favours I said yes to.
